newsitem.title: USA: Phar-Mor-ShopKo deal faced many problems.
newsitem.headline: Phar-Mor-ShopKo deal faced many problems.

text.p: The collapse of a $1 billion merger between Phar-Mor Inc and ShopKo Stores Inc marks the end of a deal fraught with problems and skepticism from the start.

The complicated financial transaction ran into trouble due to a decline in Phar-Mor's stock price, regulatory delays and uncertainty about the position of one large shareholder, said industry experts and sources familiar with the companies.
"There were many problems. Not all the pieces fell into place," said Jay Meltzer of LJR Redbook Research.

The two companies earlier Wednesday called off the deal, citing only "continuing uncertainties in consummating the transaction." The transaction, originally announced in September, set a March 31 deadline for completion.

Wall Street had disliked it from the beginning, contending the companies were dissimilar and could not achieve sizable cost savings by merging. Phar-Mor is a drugstore chain and ShopKo is a discount retailer with a healthcare subsidiary.
"I never understood it to start with. You had two businesses that had nothing to do with each other," said one investment banker who specializes in the retail sector.

Under the original plan, the two companies would have formed a new holding company called Cabot Noble Inc that would be mostly owned by ShopKo, but run primarily by Phar-Mor. The merger was to occur through a stock transaction.
But sources said the exchange of shares became a troubling issue when Phar-Mor stock, which had been trading around $8 per share when the deal was set, declined to about $5.
The companies also had not received necessary clearance from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
"It just became clear this thing was going to continue to drag on," said one source familiar with the situation.

Another sticking point was the uncertain position of key shareholder FoxMeyer Health Corp, sources said. Hamilton Morgan LLC, jointly owned by Phar-Mor chairman Robert Haft and Foxmeyer, holds 40 percent of Phar-Mor shares.
At the time the deal was announced, the companies said Foxmeyer had not reached a conclusion as to its position on the transaction.
FoxMeyer could not be reached for comment on Wednesday.
Shares of both companies gained in Wednesday trading as the cloud of uncertainty about the deal was lifted. Phar-Mor rose 1/4 to 5-1/4 and ShopKo jumped 1-3/8 to 16-5/8.
Meanwhile, shareholders of ShopKo are expected to learn more about the company's future on Thursday when it holds a telephone conference call after releasing earnings for its fiscal fourth quarter.

ShopKo is expected to move quickly with another plan in order to enable Supvalu Inc, which owns 46 percent of ShopKo, to exit its investment. Under the Phar-Mor merger, the new holding company would have bought out the bulk of Supervalu's holdings in ShopKo.

Supervalu bought ShopKo in 1971 and then sold 54 percent of its stock in a 1991 public offering. Supervalu said Wednesday it was committed to exiting its investment in ShopKo, but supported the decision to terminate the Phar-Mor deal.
